items.ask: Name every term in the master equation T_SL/W_TO = (β/α){(qS/(βW_TO))[K₁(nβW_TO/(qS))² + K₂(nβW_TO/(qS)) + C_D0 + C_DR] + P_s/V}.
items.answer: T_SL/W_TO: sea-level thrust loading. α: thrust lapse T/T_SL. β: weight fraction W/W_TO. q: dynamic pressure. n: load factor. K₁, K₂: drag polar coefficients. C_D0: zero-lift drag. C_DR: added drag (stores, gear, flaps). P_s: specific excess power.
items.cue: Thrust over weight = drag over weight + energy rate over V. Greek letters: α belongs to the engine (lapse), β to the weight (fraction).

items.ask: Outline the derivation of the master equation from the energy equation.
items.answer: 1) Power balance (T − D − R)V = W d/dt(h + V²/(2g)). 2) Divide by WV. 3) Write D = qSC_D with C_D = K₁C_L² + K₂C_L + C_D0 and C_L = nW/(qS). 4) Substitute T = αT_SL, W = βW_TO. 5) Solve for T_SL/W_TO.
items.cue: Excess power raises energy height: start with power, divide by WV, expand drag with the polar, then swap in α and β.

items.ask: State the axes of the constraint diagram and where the feasible region lies.
items.answer: x-axis: wing loading W_TO/S. y-axis: thrust loading T_SL/W_TO (power loading P_SL/W_TO for propeller aircraft). The feasible region lies above every thrust curve and to the left of the stall and landing lines.
items.cue: Wing size across, engine size up: the space above the curves and left of the stall wall is the legal zone.

items.ask: List the typical constraints drawn on a constraint diagram.
items.answer: Takeoff distance, landing distance, stall speed, cruise speed, maximum speed, climb rate or climb gradient (including one engine inoperative), service ceiling, sustained turn, acceleration (P_s), and for carrier aircraft catapult launch and approach speed.
items.cue: Follow the mission from start to finish: takeoff, climb, cruise, turn, dash, ceiling, land.

items.ask: How is the design point chosen on the constraint diagram?
items.answer: Within the feasible region, take the lowest thrust loading, then the highest wing loading at that thrust loading: the smallest engine and smallest wing that satisfy every constraint, usually at an intersection of two curves.
items.cue: Lowest, then rightmost: the corner where the cheapest engine meets the smallest wing.

items.ask: Describe the shape of each family of constraint curves versus wing loading.
items.answer: Stall and landing: vertical lines. Takeoff: straight line through the origin, rising with W/S. Cruise, turn, ceiling and maximum speed: buckets, high at low W/S (parasite term) and high at high W/S (induced term).
items.cue: Walls, ramps and buckets: stall is a wall, takeoff is a ramp, flight conditions are buckets.

items.ask: How does a constraint curve move when its flight condition moves to a higher altitude?
items.answer: It moves up: thrust lapse α falls with altitude, so more sea-level thrust is required; the bucket minimum also shifts along W/S as q changes.
items.cue: Thin air starves the engine: dividing by a smaller α lifts the whole curve.

items.ask: Which master equation terms does a sustained level turn activate, and which does a level acceleration activate?
items.answer: Sustained level turn: n = 1/cos φ above 1 in the induced term K₁n², with P_s = 0. Level acceleration: n = 1 and P_s = (V/g)dV/dt, giving the term (1/g)dV/dt in the thrust loading.
items.cue: Turns load the n² induced term; accelerations load the energy term.

items.ask: State the flight conditions for maximum range and maximum endurance for jet and propeller aircraft.
items.answer: Jet range: maximum √C_L/C_D (C_D0 = 3KC_L²). Jet endurance: maximum L/D. Propeller range: maximum L/D. Propeller endurance: maximum C_L^(3/2)/C_D (3C_D0 = KC_L²).
items.cue: Jet range takes the square root, prop endurance takes three halves; the other two share maximum L/D.

items.ask: State the assumptions behind the Breguet range equation.
items.answer: Steady level cruise (L = W, T = D); constant L/D; constant specific fuel consumption; constant V for the jet form (cruise-climb as weight falls); constant η_p for the propeller form; weight changes by fuel burn alone.
items.cue: Everything held constant except weight: the logarithm comes from integrating dW/W.

items.ask: Describe the thrust-required and power-required curves versus airspeed.
items.answer: Both U-shaped. Parasite part rises (D ∝ V², P ∝ V³); induced part falls (D ∝ 1/V², P ∝ 1/V). Minimum drag at V_md where parasite equals induced drag. Minimum power at 0.76V_md, where induced power is three times parasite power.
items.cue: A rising parasite curve and a falling induced curve. Minimum power sits left of minimum drag by the factor 3^(−1/4).

items.ask: How do the thrust-required and power-required curves move with altitude and with weight?
items.answer: Higher altitude: T_R slides right with the same minimum drag; P_R moves up and right by the factor 1/√σ. More weight: both curves move up and right (V_md ∝ √W, D_min ∝ W).
items.cue: Thin air gives the same drag at a higher true speed; extra weight lifts and stretches everything.

items.ask: Define absolute ceiling and service ceiling.
items.answer: Absolute ceiling: altitude where the maximum rate of climb reaches zero (power available just touches power required). Service ceiling: altitude where the maximum rate of climb equals 100 ft/min (0.5 m/s).
items.cue: Absolute: climb rate hits zero. Service: a hundred feet per minute left in hand.

items.ask: Give the standard liftoff, approach and touchdown speeds as multiples of stall speed.
items.answer: Liftoff V_LO ≈ 1.2V_stall; approach V_a ≈ 1.3V_stall; touchdown V_TD ≈ 1.15V_stall (civil performance convention matching the 1.44 = 1.2² ground roll formula).
items.cue: 1.2 squared gives the 1.44 in the ground roll formula; approach at 1.3, touch down at 1.15.

items.ask: For an unpowered glide, state the conditions for maximum range and for minimum sink rate.
items.answer: Maximum range: fly at (L/D)max, with glide angle tan γ = 1/(L/D) and range = h(L/D). Minimum sink rate: fly at maximum C_L^(3/2)/C_D.
items.cue: A glider borrows the propeller rules: L/D for distance, three halves for time aloft.

items.ask: Label the V-n (maneuver) diagram.
items.answer: Axes: equivalent airspeed across, load factor n up. Positive stall parabola (C_Lmax) to corner A at V_A; n_max line to dive speed V_D; vertical line at V_D; n_min line; negative stall parabola (C_Lmin). Mark V_S1 at n = 1 and cruise speed V_C.
items.cue: Parabola, roof, wall, floor, parabola: walk clockwise from the origin.

items.ask: Which parts of the V-n diagram are aerodynamically limited and which are structurally limited?
items.answer: Aerodynamically limited: the stall parabolas left of the corner speeds, where C_Lmax caps n. Structurally limited: the n_max and n_min lines and the V_D line.
items.cue: Curved edges are the wing running out of lift; straight edges are the structure's rules.

items.ask: What is special about the corner (maneuvering) speed V_A?
items.answer: It is the lowest speed at which n_max is reachable. There the aircraft has its minimum turn radius and maximum instantaneous turn rate. Below V_A the wing stalls before limit load is reached.
items.cue: The corner: tightest and fastest turn, where stall and structure meet.

items.ask: Give the limit load factors for FAR 23 normal, utility and aerobatic categories and for FAR 25 transports.
items.answer: FAR 23 normal +3.8/−1.52, utility +4.4/−1.76, aerobatic +6.0/−3.0. FAR 25: n_max = 2.1 + 24000/(W + 10000) with W in lb, bounded 2.5 ≤ n_max ≤ 3.8; n_min = −1.0.
items.cue: Positives 3.8, 4.4, 6.0. Negatives are 0.4 times the positive for normal and utility, half for aerobatic.

items.ask: Give the derived gust velocities used for the gust lines on a transport V-n diagram.
items.answer: U_de = 66 ft/s at V_B, 50 ft/s at V_C, 25 ft/s at V_D (up and down gusts, low altitude, classic FAR 25 values). Gust lines radiate from n = 1 at V = 0.
items.cue: 66, 50, 25: the gusts get gentler as the design speed gets higher.

items.ask: How does the V-n diagram change with weight and with altitude?
items.answer: Heavier: stall parabola moves right (V_S and V_A grow with √W), gust increments shrink (Δn ∝ 1/(W/S)), FAR 25 n_max falls between its bounds. Altitude: in equivalent airspeed the maneuver diagram stays fixed; in true airspeed the stall line moves right by 1/√σ.
items.cue: Weight drags the parabola right and calms the gusts; plot in V_e and the maneuver diagram holds still with altitude.

items.ask: Define limit load and ultimate load.
items.answer: Limit load: the maximum load expected in service; the structure carries it and stays free of detrimental permanent deformation. Ultimate load: 1.5 times limit load; the structure must hold it intact for at least 3 seconds.
items.cue: Limit bends and springs back; ultimate is one and a half times limit, held for three seconds.

items.ask: Write the stall speed at load factor n.
items.answer: V_s,n = √(2nW/(ρSC_Lmax)) = V_s√n.
items.cue: Pulling g makes the wing carry nW: stall speed grows with √n. The 2 comes from ½ρV².

items.ask: Give the station numbering for a two-spool separate-flow turbofan.
items.answer: 0 freestream, 1 inlet entry, 2 fan face, 13 fan exit (bypass), 2.5 low-pressure compressor exit, 3 high-pressure compressor exit, 4 combustor exit and turbine inlet, 4.5 between turbines, 5 low-pressure turbine exit, 9 core nozzle exit, 19 bypass nozzle exit.
items.cue: The core counts 0 to 9; the bypass stream puts a 1 in front: 13 after the fan, 19 at its nozzle.

items.ask: State the processes of the ideal Brayton (turbojet) cycle by station.
items.answer: 0→2 inlet ram compression (isentropic); 2→3 compressor (isentropic); 3→4 combustor heat addition at constant pressure; 4→5 turbine expansion (isentropic); 5→9 nozzle expansion to p₉ = p₀; 9→0 constant-pressure heat rejection to the atmosphere.
items.cue: Squeeze, squeeze, burn, spin, blow, cool: two isobars and four isentropic steps.

items.ask: Describe the T-s diagram of the ideal turbojet Brayton cycle.
items.answer: Isentropic steps are vertical lines. Heat addition and rejection follow isobars of slope T/c_p, which rise exponentially and spread apart toward the right. Turbine temperature drop equals compressor temperature rise (shaft work balance, equal c_p, small fuel fraction); the remaining drop to p₀ drives the nozzle.
items.cue: Verticals for isentropes, rising and spreading curves for isobars; the turbine pays the compressor, the leftover becomes jet.

items.ask: Write the Gibbs relation used to draw isobars on T-s and h-s diagrams, and the isobar slope.
items.answer: dh = T ds + v dp. On an isobar dp = 0, so dh = T ds and dT/ds = T/c_p.
items.cue: Reversible heat is T ds; v dp is flow work. The isobar slope T/c_p grows with T.

items.ask: Describe the p-v diagram of the Brayton cycle.
items.answer: Compression and expansion follow isentropes pv^γ = constant (steep curves); combustion and heat rejection are horizontal lines at constant p. The enclosed area is the net work per unit mass.
items.cue: Two flat lines and two steep curves; the loop area is the work.

items.ask: Define bypass ratio and explain why a high bypass ratio raises propulsive efficiency.
items.answer: Bypass ratio = mass flow through the fan stream (13 to 19) divided by mass flow through the core. For a given thrust ṁΔV, moving more mass with a smaller velocity increment wastes less kinetic energy ½ṁΔV², raising η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀).
items.cue: Push lots of air gently: big mass, small kick, little wasted wake energy.

items.ask: For an ideal turbojet, what do raising compressor pressure ratio and raising turbine inlet temperature do?
items.answer: Higher π_c raises thermal efficiency and lowers TSFC; specific thrust peaks at τ_c = √τ_λ/τ_r. Higher T_t4 raises specific thrust (more energy per unit mass of air), capped by turbine materials and cooling.
items.cue: Squeeze harder for efficiency, burn hotter for thrust per pound of air.

items.ask: How do real components appear on the T-s diagram compared with the ideal cycle?
items.answer: Real compression ends at higher temperature and entropy (point 3 lies right of 3s). Real turbine expansion ends at higher temperature (5 lies right of 5s). The combustor shows a total pressure drop, so p_t4 is slightly below p_t3.
items.cue: Losses push entropy right: each real point sits to the right of its ideal twin.

items.ask: List the three jet engine efficiencies and how they combine.
items.answer: Thermal η_th: rate of kinetic energy gain over fuel heat rate. Propulsive η_p: thrust power FV₀ over rate of kinetic energy gain. Overall η_o = η_th η_p = FV₀/(ṁ_f h_PR).
items.cue: Fuel to jet energy is thermal, jet energy to thrust power is propulsive; multiply for overall.

items.ask: State the Kutta condition and its role in airfoil theory.
items.answer: The flow leaves a sharp trailing edge smoothly, with finite velocity there. This fixes the circulation Γ, which sets the lift through L' = ρ∞V∞Γ.
items.cue: The trailing edge chooses Γ; Kutta-Joukowski turns Γ into lift.

items.ask: State the Helmholtz vortex theorems used in lifting-line theory and the vortex system they lead to.
items.answer: 1) A vortex filament has constant strength along its length. 2) A filament extends to infinity, closes on itself, or ends on a boundary. Result: the horseshoe vortex, a bound vortex on the wing plus two trailing vortices to infinity.
items.cue: Constant strength, endless ends: the horseshoe is the simplest legal shape.

items.ask: What does an elliptic spanwise lift distribution give?
items.answer: Uniform downwash along the span, minimum induced drag for given lift and span (e = 1), C_Di = C_L²/(πAR), and Γ(y) = Γ₀√(1 − (2y/b)²).
items.cue: Ellipse means even downwash means least induced drag.

items.ask: Write the wing root bending moment from the span load, and its value for elliptic loading.
items.answer: M_root = ∫₀^(b/2) L'(y) y dy for one semispan. For elliptic loading the semispan lift L/2 acts at 2b/(3π), so M_root = Lb/(3π).
items.cue: Load times lever arm, integrated outboard; a half-ellipse centroid sits at 4a/(3π) with a = b/2.

items.ask: Define critical Mach number and drag-divergence Mach number.
items.answer: M_cr: freestream Mach at which the local flow first reaches M = 1 somewhere on the surface. M_dd: freestream Mach where wave drag makes C_D rise steeply, commonly where dC_D/dM = 0.1. For a transport wing M_cr < M_dd < 1.
items.cue: First sonic spot, then the drag cliff; sweep and thin sections push both to higher Mach.

items.ask: What does wing sweep do aerodynamically?
items.answer: Lowers the normal Mach number M∞ cos Λ, raising M_cr and M_dd; lowers the lift-curve slope; drives spanwise flow toward the tips on an aft-swept wing (tip stall tendency); adds dihedral effect (aft sweep).
items.cue: The wing feels the cosine: slower normal flow, delayed shocks, a softer lift slope, outboard flow.

items.ask: State the assumptions of momentum (actuator disk) theory for hover.
items.answer: Infinitely thin disk with a uniform pressure jump; one-dimensional, steady, incompressible, inviscid flow; uniform induced velocity over the disk; zero swirl in the wake; far-wake static pressure equal to ambient.
items.cue: A perfect thin pump: uniform, steady, frictionless, swirl-free, with the wake back at ambient pressure.

items.ask: Give the far-wake velocity and far-wake area relative to the disk values in hover.
items.answer: Far-wake velocity w = 2v_i. By continuity the far-wake area is A/2, so the slipstream contracts.
items.cue: Half the velocity gain happens above the disk, half below: double the speed, half the area.

items.ask: Write the ideal induced velocity and ideal power in hover.
items.cue: Power is thrust times induced velocity. Power loading T/P = 1/v_i rewards low disk loading.

items.ask: How does ideal hover power scale with mass, gravity, density and disk area, and what does that mean on Mars and Titan?
items.answer: P = (mg)^(3/2)/√(2ρA). Mars: ρ about 1 to 2% of Earth sea level, g about 0.38g_E, so large fast rotors are required. Titan: ρ about 4.4 times Earth, g about 0.14g_E, so hover is far cheaper.
items.cue: Hover power loves dense air and weak gravity: Titan is a flier's paradise, Mars a flier's mountain.

items.ask: Describe dissymmetry of lift in forward flight and what limits rotor forward speed.
items.answer: The advancing blade sees ΩR + V, the retreating blade ΩR − V. Blade flapping and cyclic pitch balance the roll moment. Forward speed is capped by retreating-blade stall and reverse flow on the retreating side, and by compressibility at the advancing tip.
items.cue: One blade runs into the wind, the other runs with it: stall on the slow side, shocks on the fast side.

items.ask: How does helicopter power required vary with forward speed?
items.answer: Induced power falls (v_i ≈ T/(2ρAV)), profile power rises gently, parasite power rises as V³. Total power forms a bucket: high in hover, minimum at moderate speed (best endurance), rising again at high speed.
items.cue: The same bucket as a fixed wing: induced falls, parasite climbs with V cubed.

items.ask: Describe the reverse-flow region of a rotor in forward flight.
items.answer: On the retreating side, a circle of diameter μR passing through the hub, centred at μR/2 on the ψ = 270° azimuth, where the air meets the blade at its trailing edge first.
items.cue: Inside the circle the blade section moves slower than the forward speed: Ωr < V at ψ = 270°.

items.ask: Give the steps of the initial takeoff weight sizing loop.
items.answer: 1) Define the mission profile. 2) Guess W₀. 3) Segment weight fractions: historical for takeoff, climb, landing; Breguet for cruise and loiter. 4) W_f/W₀ = 1.06(1 − W_x/W₀). 5) W_e/W₀ from the statistical fit. 6) Compute W₀; iterate to convergence.
items.cue: Mission, guess, fractions, fuel, empty, solve, repeat: W₀ sits on both sides of the equation.

items.ask: Give the historical mission segment weight fractions for warmup and takeoff, climb, and landing.
items.answer: Warmup and takeoff 0.970; climb 0.985; landing 0.995.
items.cue: 97, 98.5, 99.5: each later phase burns a smaller slice of the airplane.

items.ask: Define wing divergence and the features that promote it.
items.answer: Static aeroelastic instability: the aerodynamic twisting moment per unit twist equals the torsional stiffness, at q_D = K_θ/(eaS). Promoted by an aerodynamic center ahead of the elastic axis, low torsional stiffness and forward sweep.
items.cue: Lift ahead of the twist axis twists the nose up, which makes more lift: a runaway loop.

items.ask: Define control (aileron) reversal.
items.answer: At q_R the nose-down wing twist caused by aileron deflection cancels the aileron lift increment, so aileron effectiveness reaches zero; above q_R the roll response reverses. Higher torsional stiffness raises q_R.
items.cue: The aileron twists the wing against itself until the two effects cancel.

items.ask: Define flutter and give two remedies.
items.answer: Dynamic aeroelastic instability: bending and torsion modes couple through aerodynamic forces and extract energy from the flow, typically as their frequencies coalesce. Remedies: mass balance moving the section CG forward toward or ahead of the elastic axis; higher torsional stiffness.
items.cue: Two modes dance in step and the airflow pays the band; move weight forward to break the rhythm.

items.ask: How does empty weight fraction trend with takeoff weight in the statistical fit?
items.answer: W_e/W₀ = AW₀^C K_vs with C a small negative exponent, so the empty weight fraction falls slowly as aircraft grow. K_vs = 1.04 for variable sweep, 1.00 for fixed sweep.
items.cue: Bigger aircraft carry relatively lighter frames, gently.

items.ask: State the assumptions that reduce the point-mass equations of motion to the vertical plane.
items.answer: Flat, nonrotating Earth; constant g; point mass; symmetric flight with zero sideslip; wings level, φ = 0; zero thrust incidence, ε = 0.
items.cue: Flat, still, symmetric, wings level: set φ = 0 and ε = 0 and the 3-D set collapses to two force equations.

items.ask: Define the angles α, γ and θ and the relation between them.
items.answer: γ: flight-path angle, velocity vector above the horizon. α: angle of attack, body x-axis above the velocity vector. θ: pitch attitude, body x-axis above the horizon. θ = α + γ (wings level).
items.cue: Pitch = attack + path: body above wind, wind above horizon.

items.ask: Give the load factor at the top of an inside loop and at the bottom of an outside loop.
items.answer: Top of an inside loop (inverted, lift toward the centre below): n = V²/(gR) − 1. Bottom of an outside loop (inverted, lift toward the centre above): n = −(1 + V²/(gR)).
items.cue: Write the force toward the centre = mV²/R; weight helps at the top, opposes at the bottom; outside loops make n negative.

items.ask: What does an energy-maneuverability chart show, and how is a minimum time to climb flown?
items.answer: Contours of specific excess power P_s and lines of constant energy height h_e on altitude versus Mach axes. The minimum time to climb (Rutowski) path passes through the points where h_e lines are tangent to P_s contours: maximum P_s on each energy level.
items.cue: Climb the energy staircase where each step pays the most power.

items.ask: Give the load factor in a level coordinated turn at 30°, 45° and 60° bank.
items.answer: n = 1/cos φ: 30° gives 1.155, 45° gives 1.414, 60° gives 2.0.
items.cue: Sixty degrees doubles your weight; forty-five gives √2.

items.ask: In a level turn, what gives the minimum turn radius and maximum turn rate?
items.answer: R = V²/(g√(n² − 1)) and ω = g√(n² − 1)/V favour high n at low V, so instantaneous turn performance peaks at the corner speed. Low W/S and high C_Lmax improve instantaneous turns; high T/W, low W/S and high eAR improve sustained turns.
items.cue: Turn hard and slow: the corner of the V-n diagram is the turning sweet spot.

items.ask: Break total aircraft drag into its components.
items.answer: Parasite (zero-lift) drag: skin friction, form (pressure) drag, interference, plus miscellaneous, leakage and protuberance drag. Induced (lift-dependent) drag. Wave drag at transonic and supersonic speeds.
items.cue: Friction, form, fit, plus lift and shocks.

items.ask: Compare the effect of trailing-edge flaps and leading-edge slats on the lift curve.
items.answer: Trailing-edge flaps shift the lift curve up and left (α_L0 more negative), raise C_Lmax and slightly lower the stall angle. Leading-edge slats extend the curve along the same slope to a higher stall angle and higher C_Lmax.
items.cue: Flaps lift the line, slats lengthen it.

items.ask: Rank trailing-edge high-lift devices by increasing airfoil ΔC_lmax.
items.answer: Plain and split flaps (0.9), slotted (1.3), Fowler (1.3c'/c), double slotted (1.6c'/c), triple slotted (1.9c'/c), where c'/c is extended chord over original chord.
items.cue: Add slots and chord: each gap re-energises the boundary layer, each extension adds area.

items.ask: Give the typical Oswald efficiency range and a straight-wing estimate for e.
items.answer: e ≈ 0.7 to 0.85. Straight wing estimate: e = 1.78(1 − 0.045AR^0.68) − 0.64.
items.cue: Real wings reach about four fifths of the ideal ellipse.

items.ask: Give the flat-plate transition Reynolds number and the wing wetted area estimate.
items.answer: Transition near Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵, so full-scale aircraft (Re in the millions) are mostly turbulent. Wing: S_wet ≈ S_exposed(1.977 + 0.52 t/c), about twice the exposed planform.
items.cue: Half a million for transition; a wing wets both faces, so about two times its exposed area.

items.ask: Distinguish C_D0 from the parasite drag force.
items.answer: C_D0 is a dimensionless coefficient set by shape, friction and wetted area ratio. Parasite drag force D₀ = qSC_D0 grows with dynamic pressure and reference area.
items.cue: The coefficient is the shape's fingerprint; the force is that fingerprint times qS.

items.ask: State the conditions for longitudinal static stability with a positive-lift trim.
items.answer: C_mα < 0 (a nose-down restoring moment as α rises) and C_m0 > 0, so C_m = 0 occurs at positive α and positive lift. Equivalently the CG lies ahead of the neutral point, SM > 0.
items.cue: The C_m line slopes down and crosses zero at positive lift.

items.ask: Define the neutral point and the static margin.
items.answer: Neutral point: the CG location where C_mα = 0, the aerodynamic center of the whole aircraft. Static margin SM = h_n − h, the distance the CG sits ahead of the neutral point in mean chords, typically 5 to 15% c̄.
items.cue: The neutral point is the airplane's ac; the margin is how far the CG sits in front of it.

items.ask: State the body-axis and control sign conventions.
items.answer: x forward, y out the right wing, z down. Positive pitch nose up, positive roll right wing down, positive yaw nose right. Positive elevator: trailing edge down, giving C_mδe < 0. Positive sideslip β: relative wind from the right.
items.cue: Right-handed with z down: nose up, right wing down and nose right are all positive.

items.ask: List the longitudinal and lateral-directional dynamic modes.
items.answer: Longitudinal: short period (fast, well damped, α and q at nearly constant V) and phugoid (slow, lightly damped, trades V and h at nearly constant α). Lateral-directional: roll subsidence (fast convergence), spiral (slow, mildly convergent or divergent), Dutch roll (oscillatory yaw and roll).
items.cue: Two longitudinal (quick bob, slow roller coaster), three lateral (roll, spiral, Dutch roll).

items.ask: List the main contributors to a stabilizing dihedral effect, C_lβ < 0.
items.answer: Geometric dihedral, wing sweepback, a high wing position, and a vertical tail above the CG.
items.cue: Anything that lifts the upwind wing: dihedral, sweepback, high wing, tall fin.

items.ask: Where does the stick-free neutral point lie relative to the stick-fixed neutral point?
items.answer: Forward of it: a free-floating elevator weakens the tail's restoring lift, so the stick-free static margin is smaller than the stick-fixed static margin.
items.cue: A loose elevator weathervanes with the flow, softening the tail: the neutral point creeps forward.
